en: Now I shall proclaim the science of phonetics (śikṣā) according to the doctrine of Pāṇini;
one should understand it as it is taught in the scriptures, following the sequence of the treatise, as it applies to both the world and the Veda.
Although the meaning of words is well-known, it remains uncomprehended by those lacking intelligence;
therefore, I shall once again clarify the procedure for the utterance of speech.
According to the doctrine of Śambhu, sixty-three or sixty-four phonemes are recognized;
they were proclaimed by the Self-born One himself for both the Prakrit and the Saṃskṛta languages.
There are twenty-one vowels and twenty-five consonants;
the letters beginning with 'ya' are recorded as eight, and the *yamas* are recorded as four. (4)
The anusvāra and the visarga—these two are also dependent upon what follows them.
The letter *ḷ* should be understood as being "badly articulated" (*duḥspṛṣṭa*) and also as a protracted vowel (*pluta*). || 5.1 ||
The self, having come together with the intellect, joins the mind with the desire to speak;
the mind strikes the fire of the body, which impels the vital air.
The vital air (māruta) moving within the chest produces a deep tone;
that is associated with the morning libation (prātaḥsavana) and rests upon the Gāyatrī metre. || 7 ||
The pair of midday [pressings] is in the throat, following the *triṣṭubh* meter;
the third pressing is the acute accent (*tāra*) on the head, following the *jagatī* meter.
The vital air, having been forcefully expelled and striking the head, reaches the mouth and produces the phonemes;
their division is traditionally taught to be fivefold.
"By way of accent, time, place, effort, and articulation—thus have those who know the phonemes declared; understand that skillfully. (10.2)
The three accents are the acute (udātta), the grave (anudātta), and the circumflex (svarita).
Short, long, and protracted—these are the rules regarding duration when followed by a vowel (ac).
Niṣāda and Gāndhāra arise from the acute accent (udātta), while Ṛṣabha and Dhaivata arise from the grave accent (anudātta);
for Ṣaḍja, Madhyama, and Pañcama originate from the circumflex accent (svarita). || 12 ||
There are eight places for the articulation of sounds: the chest, the throat, and likewise the head; the root of the tongue, the teeth, the nose, the lips, and the palate. (13)

Luminosity (obhāva), openness (vivṛtti), the sibilants ś, ṣ, and s, the letter r, the root of the tongue (jihvāmūla), and the labio-dental spirant (upadhmāna)—this is the eightfold course of the spirants (uṣman). 14.

If there is a conjunction of both [vowels and consonants], one should know that the subsequent word begins with 'u' and so forth and ends in a vowel; any other [consonant] following a sibilant (ūṣman) is manifest. 15.3.
One should know that the letter *ha* joined with the fifth [consonants] and combined with the semivowels (*antaḥsthā*) is guttural; they say it is guttural when uncombined. (16)

The letters *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, and *ṅa* are gutturals; *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*, and *ña*, along with *ya* and *śa*, are palatals; *u*, *ū*, *va*, and *p*, *pha*, *bha*, *bh*, and *m* are labials; *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ṭ*, *ṭha*, *ḍ*, *ḍha*, *ṇ*, *ra*, and *ṣa* are retroflexes; and *ḷ*, *ḹ*, *ta*, *tha*, *da*, *dha*, *na*, *la*, and *sa* are remembered as dentals. (17)
The letter *ku* is said to be at the root of the tongue; the letter *va* is remembered by the wise as being dental-labial.
The letters *e* and *ai* are known to be palatal-velar, while *o* and *au* are remembered as velar-labial.
The half-mora of the guttural [a] belongs to the vowels ai and au;
for e and o, the mora consists of both the open and the closed [articulations]. (19)
The closed [articulation] should be known as having one mora (mātrā), while the open [articulation] has two moras.
All voiced sounds are closed, and unvoiced sounds are traditionally held to be open.
The articulation of the vowels and the sibilants is traditionally held to be fully opened (*vivṛta*).
Among those, *e* and *ai* are more open than them, and likewise *o* and *au* are more open than those two. (21)
The nose is said to be the place of articulation for the anusvāra and the *yamas*.
The *ayogavāhas* should be understood as sharing the same bases and places of articulation [as the consonants they follow]. (22)
Following the sounds produced by a lute made of bottle-gourd and the sounds of the dentals,
the labials, and the vowels, the *anusvāra* must always be applied after the letters *h*, *r*, and *ḥ*, as well as after *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s*.
One should employ the separation of the lips twice in the case of an anusvāra, a vivṛtti,
a pause, or when there are two syllables [following], as well as where there are the vowels u and o.
Just as a tigress might carry her cubs with her fangs without harming them,
being afraid of their falling or being crushed, so too should one employ the phonemes.
Just as a woman from Saurāṣṭra addresses [her husband] with the word "takram," so should the *raṅgas* be employed in the void (*khe*) with effort, as if in spokes (*arām̐*). 26.
When employing the colors of the syllables, one should not swallow the preceding syllable;
one should employ a long vowel and subsequently perform the nasalization (nāsikya).
In the heart it is one mātrā, in the head it is half a mātrā, and likewise in the nose it is half;
thus the *raṅga* consists of two mātrās.
Standing at the utkara from the heart [of the altar], sounding in harmony with the bell-metal vessel, he should strike it softly for two measures; "jaghanvām" is the illustrative example.
In the middle, one should cause the tremor to shake so that both sides become equal;
one should cause the tremor to shake like a chariot with its floral ornament—this is the illustration.
In this way, the vowels should be employed—neither indistinct nor suppressed;
by the correct application of the phonemes, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā. (31)

One who sings, one who reads too fast, one who shakes his head, one who merely copies the text while reading, one who does not understand the meaning, and one with a weak voice—these six are the lowest of reciters. (32)
Sweetness, clarity of syllables, clear enunciation of words with a melodious tone, composure, and mastery of tempo—these six are the qualities of a reciter. (33)
Doubtful, fearful, harsh, indistinct, nasalized, having the voice of a crow, reaching up to the head, and likewise lacking the proper place of articulation—(these are defects). 34.

One should not speak in a whisper, nor hurriedly, nor with delay, nor with a stammer, nor in song; nor should one speak by squeezing the words together, nor by swallowing syllables and words, nor in a dejected manner, nor with the mouth agape. (35)
In the morning, one should recite daily with a voice situated in the chest, resembling the roar of a tiger;
and at midday, with a voice situated in the throat, similar to the cry of a ruddy goose.

One should know that the third libation (*savana*) is the *tāra* [note], which is located in the head; it should always be employed with a resonance situated in the head, equal to the notes of a peacock, a swan, or a cuckoo. (37)
The semi-vowels (yaṇ) are known to be slightly unaspirated; the sibilants and *ś*, *ṣ*, and *s* (śalaḥ) are considered half-aspirated;
the remaining consonants (hal) are said to be fully aspirated. Now, understand them according to their place of articulation (anupradāna).

The vowels *na*, *ma*, and *ra* are known as nasalized (*anunāsika`); *ha*, *jha*, and *ṣa* are considered to possess resonance (*nādina`); *ya* and *ṅa* have slight resonance (*īṣannāda`); while *kha*, *pha*, and the others are aspirated (*śvāsina`). 39.
One should know that the slight breaths are the "go-dhā";
this is what Pāṇini, the son of Dākṣī, has proclaimed by which this [science] has spread over the earth. (40)
The Chandas is said to be the feet of the Veda, while the Kalpa is recited as its hands;
the Jyotiṣa is its eye, and the Nirukta is called its ear. (41)
The Śikṣā is the nose of the Veda, while Vyākaraṇa is remembered as its mouth;
therefore, by studying it together with its auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), one is glorified in the world of Brahman.
The Bull (the thumb), with its tip resting at the base of the forefinger, indicates the acute accent (udātta);
it indicates the circumflex (svarita) near the middle [of the forefinger], and the grave (dhruva) as well as the acute accent on the little finger.
One should know the *udātta* (high tone) to be on the forefinger (*pradeśinī*), the *pracaya* (continuous tone) on the middle finger,
the *nihata* (low tone) on the little finger (*kaniṣṭhikā*), and the *svarita* (circumflex tone) on the ring finger (*upakaniṣṭhikā*).

The nine positions of words are: those with the accent on the final syllable (antodātta), those with the accent on the first syllable (ādyudātta), the acute (udātta), the grave (anudātta), the low-pitched circumflex (nīcasvarita), the circumflex on the middle syllable (madhyodātta), the circumflex (svarita), those with two accents (dvyudātta), and those with three accents (tryudātta). 45.

*agniḥ*, *somaḥ*, *pra*, *vaḥ*, *vīryam*, *haviṣām*, *svaḥ*, *bṛhaspatiḥ*, *indrābṛhaspatī*, and *agniḥ* are accented on the final syllable; *somaḥ* is accented on the first syllable; *pra* is accutely accented;
*vaḥ* is gravely accented; and *vīryam* has a low svarita. 46.
Among the *havir* [vocatives], *madhyodāttaṃ svaḥ* is circumflex (*svarita*);
*bṛhaspatiḥ* has two acute accents (*dvyudātta*); and *indrābṛhaspatī* has three acute accents (*tryudātta*). || 47 ||

The *anudātta* (unaccented) is to be known as being in the heart; the *udātta* (accented) is declared to be at the top of the head; the *svarita* (circumflex) belongs to the root of the ear; and the *pracaya* (continuous) is remembered as being throughout the entire mouth. || 48 ||
The blue jay speaks with one mora, while the crow indeed speaks with two moras;
the peacock cries with three moras, and the mongoose with half a mora. (49)
That which has come from a false teacher, is burnt, discolored,
or consumed— there is no liberation through its recitation, just as there is none from the sin of a venomous serpent.
The Veda shines when it has emerged from a true source, is clear, follows its own tradition, is well-structured, and is uttered with a beautiful voice by a skilled speaker. (51)
A mantra deficient in accent or phoneme, when incorrectly employed, does not convey its intended meaning;
that thunderbolt of speech destroys the sacrificer, just as Indra’s enemy [Prajāpati] was destroyed due to a fault in accent. 52.
One who is illiterate has a shortened lifespan; one with a discordant voice is afflicted by disease;
and those who have not been wounded by weapons find a thunderbolt falling upon their head.
But he who studies [the Veda] lacking the hand-gestures (mudrās), devoid of proper accents and phonemes, being consumed by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, goes to a base womb. || 54 ||
He who studies the Veda with his hand, correctly joined with its accents, phonemes, and meanings,
is purified by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas and is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Śaṅkara bestowed the Śāṅkarī [grammar] upon the wise son of Dakṣī; having extracted it from all forms of speech, he gave it to the Goddess Vāc—such is the established tradition. (56)
Salutations to that Pāṇini, by whom, having received the traditional collection of phonemes from Maheśvara, the entire science of grammar was proclaimed. (57)
Salutation to that Pāṇini, by whom the speech of men has been washed clean with the waters of his words and the darkness born of ignorance has been shattered. 58.
Salutations to that Pāṇini, by whom the eye of the world blinded by ignorance was opened with the ointment-stick of knowledge. 59.

The twice-born who, being ever diligent, recites here this [hymn] that has issued forth from the face of the Three-eyed One, becomes possessed of wealth, grain, cattle, sons, and fame, and enjoys incomparable happiness in heaven—yes, in heaven! (60)
Then Śikṣā, Ātmadātta, and Hakāra; likewise Svarāṇāṃ, Yathā, Gīti, Acaspṛṣṭa, Udātta, and Cāṣa; while Śaṅkara is the eleventh. (61)
Thus ends the Pāṇinīya Śikṣā.
